blocks.text: Erythroblastosis foetalis is a haemolytic disease of the foetus or newborn caused by Rh incompatibility between an Rh-negative pregnant mother and an Rh-positive foetus.

It occurs when an Rh-negative mother (dd) carries an Rh-positive baby (DD or Dd). Foetal blood may enter the mother's blood; exposed to the foetal Rh antigens, she makes anti-Rh antibodies. These cross the placenta into the foetal blood and destroy the foetal red cells, causing haemolytic anaemia and other serious complications.

blocks.alt: Three panels, each a pink oval for an Rh-negative (dd) mother with an Rh-positive baby inside. First pregnancy: a few of the baby's red cells are in the mother's blood at birth. After the first birth: Y-shaped anti-Rh antibodies fill her blood. Next pregnancy: antibodies cross the placenta to the baby, destroying its red cells. A green box gives prevention with anti-Rh serum.

blocks.long_description: Erythroblastosis foetalis arises when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive foetus. Some foetal red cells, most often at birth, enter her blood; her immune system responds by making anti-Rh antibodies, which stay for life. In a later pregnancy with an Rh-positive foetus these antibodies cross the placenta and destroy foetal red cells, causing haemolytic anaemia, jaundice from bilirubin, an enlarged liver and spleen, and in severe cases miscarriage or stillbirth. Giving the mother anti-Rh serum in early pregnancy and immediately after birth destroys any foetal red cells in her blood before her immune system is sensitised.

items: In severe cases the destruction of foetal red cells can cause miscarriage or stillbirth.
If the foetus survives, its liver and spleen enlarge as they try to make more red cells.
Breakdown of red cells produces bilirubin, which builds up and causes jaundice (yellow skin and eyes); high bilirubin can also damage brain cells.
The surviving baby's blood is replaced with Rh-negative blood free of anti-Rh antibodies.

blocks.title: Tidbit: prevention with anti-Rh serum
blocks.text: When Rh incompatibility is possible, the mother is given an injection of Rh antiserum (serum containing anti-Rh antibodies) in early pregnancy and immediately after birth. It destroys any of the baby's red cells that have crossed into her blood before they can sensitise her immune system.

blocks.title: Tidbit: ABO incompatibility can protect
blocks.text: If an O-negative mother carries an A-positive or B-positive baby, any foetal red cells entering her blood are quickly destroyed by her existing anti-A or anti-B antibodies, before she can form anti-Rh antibodies.

blocks.prompt: An Rh-negative woman marries an Rh-positive man whose father was Rh-negative. Give the possible genotypes and the chance that their child is affected.
blocks.explanation: Woman dd; the man got d from his dd father, so he is Dd; his mother is DD or Dd. Each child has a 1/2 chance of being Dd (Rh-positive) and 1/2 of dd. An Rh-positive child is at risk only once the mother has been sensitised, usually not in the first such pregnancy, and anti-Rh serum can prevent it.

items: Rh-negative mother + Rh-positive foetus: her anti-Rh antibodies destroy foetal red cells.
Effects: anaemia, enlarged liver and spleen, jaundice, possible brain damage, miscarriage.
Prevention: anti-Rh serum early in pregnancy and right after birth.
